title: Women's voices today
hook: women serve as granthis and ragis, and Sikhs discuss where women may do kirtan

segments.voice: Yesterday, hakk, and your line was rights for all. Did you speak up for someone? Today, a question Sikhs are still talking through among themselves. Day one thousand thirty-five.

Why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? That question is Guru Nanak's, in the Guru Granth Sahib. Hold it in mind. A gurdwara, an ordinary evening. A woman sits behind the Guru Granth Sahib, reading aloud, waving the chaur over the open pages. Later, a group of women sit at the harmonium and sing the evening hymns. In this hall, it's ordinary. And yet, in some places, Sikhs are still discussing where women's kirtan groups may sing. Today is about a teaching that is clear, and a conversation that isn't finished.
screen: `WHY CALL HER LESSER?` → `A WOMAN AT THE GURU'S SIDE.` → `A CONVERSATION NOT FINISHED.`

segments.voice: First, the line. At Ang 473 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in a hymn of Guru Nanak, the Guru says that we are born of woman, we marry woman, through woman friendships and families are made, and then he asks: why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? The question is the teaching. Second, the practice today. Sikh women serve as granthis, reading from and caring for the Guru Granth Sahib, and as ragis, singing kirtan. Women serve on gurdwara committees, cook and serve langar, and take part in the Panj Pyare in some congregations, while others keep that role for men. The Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, opens the main parts of gurdwara life to Sikh men and women alike. Third, the open question. At Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the kirtan in the inner sanctum has traditionally been sung by men's groups, and some Sikhs have asked that women's groups sing there too. Some point to Ang 473 and say the Gurus' teaching on equality already settles it. Others say a change at that place should come through the Panth's own institutions, in their own time. The question has been raised more than once, and it is still being discussed. Fourth, the shape of it. The teaching is clear, and the practice is wide. One place, and some roles, are still under discussion. That is today's line: a conversation open. It's honest to say it's open, and honest to say whose words both sides are reaching for.
screen: `ANG 473: WHY CALL HER LESSER?` · `GRANTHIS, RAGIS, COMMITTEES, LANGAR.` · `KIRTAN AT HARMANDIR SAHIB?` · `CLEAR TEACHING, OPEN QUESTION.` · then, large: `A CONVERSATION OPEN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with an open conversation. Sit, and let your breath settle. Think of a conversation in your own life that isn't finished yet. In your family, your work, your community. Something people keep coming back to. Don't try to win it right now. Just notice it. Breathe in, and hear the strongest point on one side. Breathe out, and hear the strongest point on the other. Notice where you lean, and notice what you might still be missing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan. The singing of the Guru's hymns, led today by women as granthis and ragis too, with the question of where women's groups may sing still open. Today's word.
Your line: a conversation open. Today, notice one conversation that's still open around you, and listen to the side you usually skip before you add anything. Day one thousand thirty-five.
